newsitem.title: USA: U.S property CEOs worried about competition -- study.
newsitem.headline: U.S property CEOs worried about competition -- study.

text.p: The most important strategic issue facing the U.S. property-casualty industry is the industry's increasingly competitive environment, according to a new survey of property-casualty chief executives.
This new focus on competition represents a shift from a similar survey conducted in 1994 that found the regulatory environment to be the most important strategic issue.
The survey, conducted by Tillinghast-Towers Perrin and Towers Perrin Reinsurance in late 1996, was mailed to 300 of the largest U.S. property-casualty insurance companies.
The findings are based on confidential responses received from 52 of them, Towers Perrin said.
Respondents have statutory surplus ranging from $50 million to well over $1 billion.
Mutual companies represented about 40 percent of respondents, with the balance split among stock companies, foreign-owned and others.
Other strategic issues identified by the chief executives in this latest survey, in order of importance, were control of claim expenses, control of operating expenses and management of distribution.
Regulatory issues were ranked seventh, the firm said.
"The industry is becoming destabilized," said Howard Dempster, a Philadelphia-based consultant with Tillinghast-Towers Perrin.
Excess capacity is holding rates down, new competitors are entering the business and merger activity is consolidating the industry, he said.
"CEOs must recognize the fact that in this rapidly changing environment, business as usual is a liquidation policy," he said.

"For example, mergers and acquisitions are now a viable growth strategy. It is time for them to rethink the business and to make the quantum leaps needed to succeed. Incremental measures won't suffice," he said.
Large personal lines companies named management of distribution as their top concern, the firm said.
Management of catastrophe risk and exposures was ranked second by smaller companies and less profitable companies.
Commercial line insurers ranked increased competition as the top issue.
Control of operating expenses was ranked second by all but the less profitable commercial line writers.
The survey also asked CEOs to name the North American property-casualty insurer best positioned to deal with the issues facing the industry in both personal and commercial lines, the firm said.
As in the 1994 survey, the company named most often for personal lines was State Farm.
State Farm's size, market share, strong capital base, distribution system, low cost position and loyal customer base were cited as the reasons.
American International Group Inc was the insurer mentioned most frequently for commercial lines, as in 1994.
Its global capabilities, diversified operations, consistent results, operating cost advantages and strong capital position were cited.
